- If sentiment is positive (≥0.2) and forecast is flat or rising slowly, model tends to under-forecast sharp upward moves; adjust upward by 2–5% for early spikes.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.0) and forecast is rising, model often over-optimistic; cap upward slope at 0.5–1.0% per day to avoid overshoot.
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days falling from peak), model often fails to correct; reduce forecast slope by 10–20% in subsequent days.
- If forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows sudden drop (e.g., 10–15% drop from peak), model often lags; add 1–2 days of downward correction in forecast.
- For sentiment history with multiple 0.2+ spikes, model tends to over-forecast later days; apply exponential decay to forecast slope (e.g., 0.8x previous slope) after 3+ positive sentiment days.
- If forecast is flat or slightly rising and true outcome shows volatility, model often misses volatility; add ±1–2% noise to forecast for volatile periods.
- When sentiment is 0.0 and forecast is rising, model often overestimates; reduce forecast by 1–3% for 2–3 days if no sentiment change.
- If forecast is rising and true outcome shows sharp peak followed by drop, model often overshoots; cap forecast at 10–15% above peak for 2–3 days.
